paragraphs: As therefore the Holy Scriptures in many places not only admit but actually require a different explanation from what seems to be the literal one, it seems to me that they ought to be reserved for the last place in mathematical discussions. For they, like nature, owe their origin to the Divine Word; … it was necessary, however, in Holy Scripture, in order to accommodate itself to the understanding of the majority, to say many things which apparently differ from the precise meaning. Nature, on the contrary, is inexorable and unchangeable, and cares not whether her hidden causes and modes of working are intelligible to the human understanding or not, and never deviates on that account from her prescribed laws. It appears to me therefore that no effect of nature, which experience places before our eyes, or is the necessary conclusion derived from evidence, should be rendered doubtful by passages of Scripture which contain thousands of words admitting of various interpretations …

Since two truths can obviously never contradict each other, it is the part of wise interpreters of Holy Scripture to take the pains to find out the real meaning of its statements, in accordance with the conclusions regarding nature which are quite certain, either from the clear evidence of sense or from necessary demonstration. … Who will set bounds to man's understanding? Who can assure us that everything that can be known in the world is known already? …

I am inclined to think that the authority of Holy Scripture is intended to convince men of those truths which are necessary for their salvation, and which being far above man's understanding cannot be made credible by any learning, or any other means than revelation by the Holy Spirit. But that the same God who has endowed us with senses, reason, and understanding, does not permit us to use them, and desires to acquaint us in any other way with such knowledge as we are in a position to acquire for ourselves by means of those faculties, that it seems to me I am not bound to believe, especially concerning those sciences about which the Holy Scriptures contain only small fragments and varying conclusions; and this is precisely the case with astronomy, of which there is so little that the planets are not even all enumerated.
X1.attribution: Galileo Galilei, Italian mathematician and astronomer, letter to Benedetto Castelli, a Benedictine monk who taught mathematics at the University of Pisa, December 21, 1613

paragraphs: If woman is made to please and to be in subjection to man, she ought to make herself pleasing in his eyes and not provoke him to anger … A man has no one but himself to consider, and so long as he does right he may defy public opinion; but when a woman does right her task is only half finished, and what people think of her matters as much as what she really is. …

The children's health depends in the first place on the mother's, and the early education of man is also in a woman's hands; his morals, his passions, his tastes, his pleasures, his happiness itself, depend on her. A woman's education must therefore be planned in relation to man. To be pleasing in his sight, to win his respect and love, to train him in childhood, to tend him in manhood, to counsel and console, to make his life pleasant and happy, these are the duties of woman for all time, and this is what she should be taught while she is young.
items.attribution: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, philosopher born in Geneva who lived mostly in France, Emile, a book in the form of a novel about the education of a boy named Emile, 1762. This passage comes from Book V, about the education of the young woman Emile will marry.

paragraphs: Custom may familiarise mankind with the violation of their natural rights to such an extent, that even among those who have lost or been deprived of these rights, no one thinks of reclaiming them, or is even conscious that they have suffered any injustice. …

Certain of these violations (of natural right) have escaped the notice of philosophers and legislators, even while concerning themselves zealously to establish the common rights of individuals of the human race, and in this way to lay the foundation of political institutions. For example, have they not all violated the principle of the equality of rights in tranquilly depriving one-half of the human race of the right of taking part in the formation of laws by the exclusion of women from the rights of citizenship? …

But the rights of men result simply from the fact that they are rational, sentient beings, susceptible of acquiring ideas of morality, and of reasoning concerning those ideas. Women having, then, the same qualities, have necessarily the same rights. Either no individual of the human species has any true rights, or all have the same; and he or she who votes against the rights of another, whatever may be his or her religion, colour, or sex, has by that fact abjured his own.
items.attribution: Marquis de Condorcet, French mathematician and philosopher, "On the Admission of Women to the Rights of Citizenship," essay published in a Paris journal, July 1790

paragraphs: Population, when unchecked, increases in a geometrical ratio. Subsistence increases only in an arithmetical ratio. … By that law of our nature which makes food necessary to the life of man, the effects of these two unequal powers must be kept equal. …

The preventive check appears to operate in some degree through all the ranks of society in England. … The sons of tradesmen and farmers are exhorted not to marry, and generally find it necessary to pursue this advice till they are settled in some business or farm that may enable them to support a family. These events may not, perhaps, occur till they are far advanced in life. …

The labourer who earns eighteen pence a day and lives with some degree of comfort as a single man, will hesitate a little before he divides that pittance among four or five, which seems to be but just sufficient for one. … he must feel conscious, if he thinks at all, that should he have a large family, and any ill luck whatever, no degree of frugality, no possible exertion of his manual strength could preserve him from the heart-rending sensation of seeing his children starve, or of forfeiting his independence, and being obliged to the parish* for their support.

paragraphs: When we began this enterprise we looked forward only to those difficulties to which its extent and the variety of the subjects to be treated would give rise; but this proved to be a momentary illusion and we soon beheld the multitude of material obstacles which we had foreseen reenforced by an infinite number of intellectual hindrances for which we were in no way prepared. …

Among all the various forms of persecution inflicted, in all times and among all peoples, upon those who have yielded to the dangerous temptation of endeavoring to inscribe their names on the list of benefactors of the human race, there are almost none which have not been directed against us. … During twenty consecutive years we can look back to hardly a moment of rest. … How often have we risen uncertain whether, yielding to the cries of slander, we should not tear ourselves away from our relatives, friends, and fellow-citizens to seek the necessary peace and protection tendered us beneath a foreign sky. …

May general education advance with such rapidity during the coming twenty years that there will be in a thousand of our pages scarce a line that will not then be known to everybody! It is the duty of the masters of the world to hasten this happy consummation. It is they who extend or contract the horizon of knowledge. Happy the time when they come to understand that their safety lies in ruling over educated men! Attacks on the lives of sovereigns have always been made by blind fanatics. How can we complain of our difficulties and regret our years of labor if we can flatter ourselves that we have done even a little to weaken this mad spirit which is so hostile to social peace, and have encouraged our fellow-beings to love one another, tolerate one another, and recognize the superiority of universal reason over all individual systems which can only inspire hate, animosity, and disorder …

paragraphs: France had long been the most literary of all the nations of Europe; although her literary men had never exhibited such intellectual powers as they displayed about the middle of the eighteenth century, or occupied such a position as that which they then assumed. … They were invested with no authority whatever, and filled no public offices in a society crowded with public officers; yet they did not, like the greater part of their brethren in Germany, keep entirely aloof from the arena of politics and retire into the regions of pure philosophy and polite literature. They busied themselves incessantly with matters appertaining to government, and this was, in truth, their special occupation. …

They all agreed that it was expedient to substitute simple and elementary rules, deduced from reason and natural law, for the complicated traditional customs which governed the society of their time. …

The sight of so many unjust or absurd privileges, the burden of which was more and more felt whilst their cause was less and less understood, urged, or rather precipitated, the minds of one and all towards the idea of the natural equality of man's condition. …

They had no idea of the perils which always accompany the most needful revolutions; they had not even a presentiment of them, for the complete absence of all political liberty had the effect of rendering the transaction of public affairs not only unknown to them, but even invisible. … Thus they became far more bold in innovation, more fond of generalising and of systems, more disdainful of the wisdom of antiquity, and still more confident in their individual reason, than is commonly to be seen in authors who write speculative books on politics.
The same state of ignorance opened to them the ears and hearts of the people. …
X8.attribution: Alexis de Tocqueville, French historian and politician, The Old Regime and the Revolution, 1856

paragraphs: There are and can exist but two ways of investigating and discovering truth. The one hurries on rapidly from the senses and particulars to the most general axioms, and from them, as principles and their supposed indisputable truth, derives and discovers the intermediate axioms. This is the way now in use. The other constructs its axioms from the senses and particulars, by ascending continually and gradually, till it finally arrives at the most general axioms, which is the true but unattempted way. …

Those who have treated of the sciences have been either empirics or dogmatical. The former like ants only heap up and use their store, the latter like spiders spin out their own webs. The bee, a mean between both, extracts matter from the flowers of the garden and the field, but works and fashions it by its own efforts. The true labor of philosophy resembles hers …

paragraphs: The first was never to accept anything for true which I did not clearly know to be such; that is to say, carefully to avoid precipitancy and prejudice, and to comprise nothing more in my judgement than what was presented to my mind so clearly and distinctly as to exclude all ground of doubt.
The second, to divide each of the difficulties under examination into as many parts as possible, and as might be necessary for its adequate solution.

The third, to conduct my thoughts in such order that, by commencing with objects the simplest and easiest to know, I might ascend by little and little, and, as it were, step by step, to the knowledge of the more complex …

The long chains of simple and easy reasonings by means of which geometers are accustomed to reach the conclusions of their most difficult demonstrations, had led me to imagine that all things, to the knowledge of which man is competent, are mutually connected in the same way …

paragraphs: … I profess both to learn and to teach anatomy, not from books but from dissections; not from the positions of philosophers but from the fabric of nature …

But what remains to be said upon the quantity and source of the blood which thus passes, is of so novel and unheard-of character, that I not only fear injury to myself from the envy of a few, but I tremble lest I have mankind at large for my enemies, so much doth wont and custom, that become as another nature, and doctrine once sown and that hath struck deep root, and respect for antiquity influence all men … I frequently and seriously bethought me, and long revolved in my mind, what might be the quantity of blood which was transmitted, in how short a time its passage might be effected, and the like; and not finding it possible that this could be supplied by the juices of the ingested aliment without the veins on the one hand becoming drained, and the arteries on the other getting ruptured through the excessive charge of blood, unless the blood should somehow find its way from the arteries into the veins, and so return to the right side of the heart; I began to think whether there might not be a MOTION, AS IT WERE, IN A CIRCLE. paragraphs: A Frenchman who arrives in London, will find philosophy, like everything else, very much changed there. He had left the world a plenum, and he now finds it a vacuum. At Paris the universe is seen composed of vortices of subtile matter; but nothing like it is seen in London. In France, it is the pressure of the moon that causes the tides; but in England it is the sea that gravitates towards the moon … According to your Cartesians*, everything is performed by an impulsion, of which we have very little notion; and according to Sir Isaac Newton, it is by an attraction, the cause of which is as much unknown to us. …

This famous Newton, this destroyer of the Cartesian system, died in March, anno 1727. His countrymen honoured him in his lifetime, and interred him as though he had been a king who had made his people happy. …

Descartes was injuriously accused of being an atheist, the last refuge of religious scandal: and he who had employed all the sagacity and penetration of his genius, in searching for new proofs of the existence of a God, was suspected to believe there was no such Being. …

It was his** peculiar felicity, not only to be born in a country of liberty, but in an age when all scholastic impertinences were banished from the world. Reason alone was cultivated, and mankind could only be his pupil, not his enemy.

MEN being, as has been said, by nature, all free, equal, and independent, no one can be put out of this estate, and subjected to the political power of another, without his own consent. …

paragraphs: In every government there are three sorts of powers. … By virtue of the first, the prince, or magistrate, enacts temporary or perpetual laws, and amends or abrogates those that have been already enacted. By the second, he makes peace or war, sends or receives embassies, establishes the public security, and provides against invasions. By the third, he punishes criminals, or determines the disputes that arise between individuals. …

When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, or in the same body of magistrates, there can be no liberty, because apprehensions may arise lest the same monarch or senate should enact tyrannical laws, and then execute them in a tyrannical manner.
Again, there is no liberty if the judiciary power be not separated from the legislative and executive. …

There would be an end of everything, were the same man, or the same body, whether of the nobles or of the people, to exercise those three powers, — that of enacting laws, that of executing the public resolutions, and that of trying the suits of individuals.

Most kingdoms in Europe enjoy a moderate government, because the prince who is invested with the two first powers leaves the third to his subjects. In Turkey*, where these three powers are united in the sultan's person, the subjects groan under the most dreadful oppression.
P5.attribution: Montesquieu (Charles-Louis de Secondat, baron de Montesquieu), French noble and former judge, The Spirit of the Laws, Book XI, 1748
P5.translation: English translation as printed in James Harvey Robinson and Charles A. Beard, Readings in Modern European History, vol. 1 (1908); adapted

paragraphs: It is evident that the intent of punishments is not to torment a sensitive being nor to undo a crime already committed. … Can the groans of a tortured wretch recall the time past or reverse the crime he has committed?
The end of punishment therefore is no other than to prevent others from committing the like offense. …
No man can be judged a criminal until he be found guilty; nor can society take from him the public protection until it has been proved that he has violated the conditions on which it was granted. …

The punishment of death is pernicious to society from the examples of barbarity it affords. … Is it not absurd that the laws which detect and punish homicide should, in order to prevent murder, publicly commit murder themselves? …

How happy were mankind if laws were now to be first formed, now that we see on the thrones of Europe benevolent monarchs, friends to the virtues of peace, to the arts and sciences, fathers of their people, though crowned, yet citizens …
P6.attribution: Cesare Beccaria, Italian legal reformer from Milan, then ruled by the Habsburgs of Austria, On Crimes and Punishments, 1764
P6.translation: English translation published in Edinburgh in 1788, as printed in James Harvey Robinson and Charles A. Beard, Readings in Modern European History, vol. 1 (1908); adapted

paragraphs: She was rich enough to make her house the rendezvous of literature and the arts; and seeing that this would afford her old age an amusing society and a respectable character in the world, Madame Geoffrin* had established at her house two weekly dinners, one on Monday for artists, another on Wednesday for men of letters. It is very remarkable that, though this woman had no knowledge either of the arts or of literature, and had never learned anything thoroughly in her life, yet, when placed in the midst of these two societies, she did not seem out of place. …

But her great art consisted in presiding, in watching, in keeping up her authority over two classes of men who are naturally fond of freedom. She set bounds, however, to this liberty, and by a word or a gesture, as by an invisible thread, could recall any one who attempted to escape. …

Nothing flattered her more than her intercourse with the great. She seldom visited them at their own houses (there she was not at her ease), but she had the art of drawing them to hers by a secret and imperceptible flattery.
P7.attribution: Jean-François Marmontel, French writer and a regular guest at Madame Geoffrin's house in Paris in the 1750s and 1760s, Memoirs, written in the 1790s and published in 1804

paragraphs: The coffee house must not be dismissed with a cursory mention. It might indeed at that time have been not improperly called a most important political institution. No Parliament had sat for years. The municipal council of the City had ceased to speak the sense of the citizens. Public meetings, harangues, resolutions, and the rest of the modern machinery of agitation had not yet come into fashion. Nothing resembling the modern newspaper existed. In such circumstances the coffee houses were the chief organs through which the public opinion of the metropolis vented itself.

The first of these establishments had been set up by a Turkey merchant, who had acquired among the Mahometans* a taste for their favourite beverage. … Every man of the upper or middle class went daily to his coffee house to learn the news and to discuss it. … The Court had long seen with uneasiness the growth of this new power in the state. An attempt had been made, during Danby's administration, to close the coffee houses. But men of all parties missed their usual places of resort so much that there was an universal outcry. … Nobody was excluded from these places who laid down his penny at the bar. Yet every rank and profession, and every shade of religious and political opinion, had its own headquarters.
P8.attribution: Thomas Babington Macaulay, British historian and politician, The History of England from the Accession of James II, vol. 1, 1848. Macaulay is describing London in 1685.

paragraphs: In times when industry and the arts flourish, men are kept in perpetual occupation, and enjoy, as their reward, the occupation itself, as well as those pleasures which are the fruit of their labour. …

Another advantage of industry and of refinements in the mechanical arts, is, that they commonly produce some refinements in the liberal … The same age which produces great philosophers and politicians, renowned generals and poets, usually abounds with skilful weavers, and ship-carpenters. …

The more these refined arts advance, the more sociable men become … They flock into cities; love to receive and communicate knowledge; to show their wit or their breeding; their taste in conversation or living, in clothes or furniture. Curiosity allures the wise; vanity the foolish; and pleasure both. Particular clubs and societies are everywhere formed: both sexes meet in an easy and sociable manner; and the tempers of men, as well as their behaviour, refine apace. … Thus industry, knowledge, and humanity, are linked together, by an indissoluble chain, and are found, from experience as well as reason, to be peculiar to the more polished, and, what are commonly denominated, the more luxurious ages.

Nor are these advantages attended with disadvantages that bear any proportion to them. The more men refine upon pleasure, the less will they indulge in excesses of any kind; because nothing is more destructive to true pleasure than such excesses.
P9.attribution: David Hume, Scottish philosopher and historian, "Of Refinement in the Arts," essay first published in 1752 under the title "Of Luxury"

paragraphs: A propos of distempers, I am going to tell you a thing that will make you wish yourself here. The small-pox, so fatal, and so general amongst us, is here entirely harmless, by the invention of ingrafting, which is the term they give it. There is a set of old women, who make it their business to perform the operation, every autumn, in the month of September, when the great heat is abated. … the old woman comes with a nutshell full of the matter of the best sort of small-pox, and asks what vein you please to have opened. She immediately rips open that you offer to her, with a large needle, (which gives you no more pain than a common scratch) and puts into the vein as much matter as can ly upon the head of her needle …

The children or young patients play together all the rest of the day, and are in perfect health to the eighth. Then the fever begins to seize them, and they keep their beds two days, very seldom three. … Every year thousands undergo this operation … There is no example of any one that has died in it; and you may believe I am well satisfied of the safety of this experiment, since I intend to try it on my dear little son.

I am patriot enough to take pains to bring this useful invention into fashion in England; and I should not fail to write to some of our doctors very particularly about it, if I knew any one of them that I thought had virtue enough to destroy such a considerable branch of their revenue, for the good of mankind.
P11.attribution: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, English writer and wife of the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, letter to a friend in England, written from the Ottoman city of Adrianople (Edirne), April 1, 1717; first published in 1763
P11.translation: Text from Letters of the Right Honourable Lady M—y W—y M—e (London, 1790); adapted

paragraphs: Yet the change between 1700 and 1800 was astonishing. England not only produced food for a population that had doubled itself, as well as grain for treble the number of horses, but during the first part of the period became, as M. de Lavergne* has said, the granary of Europe. … The standard of living improved. Instead of the salted carcases of half-starved and aged oxen, fresh meat began to be eaten by the peasantry. …

The great changes which English agriculture witnessed as the eighteenth century advanced, and particularly after the accession of George III. (1760), are, broadly speaking, identified with Jethro Tull, Lord Townshend, Bakewell of Dishley, Arthur Young, and Coke of Norfolk. With their names are associated the chief characteristics in the farming progress of the period, which may be summed up in the adoption of improved methods of cultivation, the introduction of new crops, the reduction of stock-breeding to a science, the provision of increased facilities of communication and of transport, and the enterprise and outlay of capitalist landlords and tenant-farmers. … Without the substitution of separate occupation for the ancient system of common cultivation, this agricultural progress was impossible. But in carrying out the necessary changes, rural society was convulsed, and its general conditions revolutionised. The divorce of the peasantry from the soil, and the extinction of commoners, open-field farmers, and eventually of small freeholders, were the heavy price which the nation ultimately paid for the supply of bread and meat to its manufacturing population.
P12.attribution: Rowland E. Prothero (later Lord Ernle), British historian and politician, English Farming, Past and Present, 1912

footnotes.text: Léonce de Lavergne, a French writer on farming in the 1800s

glossary.d: farms held and worked by a single owner or tenant
the old village system in which each family farmed scattered strips of land side by side with its neighbors
villagers with rights to graze animals and gather wood on village land
farmers who owned their own land

paragraphs: We have remarked that men have granted preeminence to one of their equals, in expectation that he should do them certain services. These services consist in the maintenance of the laws, a strict execution of justice, an employment of his whole powers to prevent any corruption of manners, and defending the State against its enemies. It is the duty of this magistrate to pay attention to agriculture; it should be his care that provisions for the nation should be in abundance, and that commerce and industry should be encouraged. He is a perpetual sentinel, who must watch the acts and the conduct of the enemies of the State. …
Princes and monarchs, therefore, are not invested with supreme authority that they may, with impunity, riot in debauchery and voluptuousness. …
But neither politics nor the army can prosper if the finances are not kept in the greatest order, and if the prince himself be not a prudent economist. …

The monarch is only the first servant of the State, who is obliged to act with probity and prudence, and to remain as totally disinterested as if he were each moment liable to render an account of his administration to his fellow-citizens.
P14.attribution: Frederick II, king of Prussia from 1740 to 1786, "Essay on the Forms of Government and on the Duties of Sovereigns," written in French in 1777
P14.translation: Translated by Thomas Holcroft in Posthumous Works of Frederic II, King of Prussia, vol. 5 (London, 1789), as printed in James Harvey Robinson and Charles A. Beard, Readings in Modern European History, vol. 1 (1908); adapted

glossary.d: bad behavior and loss of good morals
wild living and a love of pleasure
not acting for his own gain

paragraphs: A great many foreigners, from various causes, cannot have a just notion of the authority that is exercised in France by public opinion. They cannot comprehend the nature of an invisible power which, destitute of treasury, of guards and armies, dictates its laws in the capital, in the court, and even in the king's palace. Nevertheless nothing is more true nor more remarkable …

I will go still farther: it is the ascendency of public opinion that opposes more obstacles in France to the abuse of power than any other consideration whatsoever. Yes, it is entirely by that opinion, and the esteem in which it is still held, that the nation has a kind of influence, by having it in its power to reward with praise, or punish with contempt. If ever that opinion is entirely despised, or if it ever grows too weak, then liberty will lose its principal support, and there will be a greater necessity than ever that the sovereign should be virtuous and his ministers moderate.
P15.attribution: Jacques Necker, banker from Geneva who served as director-general of finances for King Louis XVI of France from 1777 to 1781, On the Administration of the Finances of France, 1784
P15.translation: English translation as printed in James Harvey Robinson and Charles A. Beard, Readings in Modern European History, vol. 1 (1908); adapted

paragraphs: There are some who say that, if we treated with paternal indulgence those erring brethren who pray to God in bad French [instead of bad Latin], we should be putting weapons in their hands, and would once more witness the battles of Jarnac, Moncontour, Coutras, Dreux, and St. Denis*. I do not know anything about this, as I am not a prophet; but it seems to me an illogical piece of reasoning to say: "These men rebelled when I treated them ill, therefore they will rebel when I treat them well." …

The Huguenots, it is true, have been as inebriated with fanaticism and stained with blood as we. But are this generation as barbaric as their fathers? Have not time, the progress of reason, good books, and the humanising influence of society had an effect on the leaders of these people? And do we not perceive that the aspect of nearly the whole of Europe has been changed within the last fifty years? …

The rage that is inspired by the dogmatic spirit and the abuse of the Christian religion, wrongly conceived, has shed as much blood and led to as many disasters in Germany, England, and even Holland, as in France. Yet religious difference causes no trouble to-day in those States. The Jew, the Catholic, the Greek, the Lutheran, the Calvinist, the Anabaptist, the Socinian, the Memnonist, the Moravian, and so many others, live like brothers in these countries, and contribute alike to the good of the social body. …
P16.attribution: Voltaire, French writer, Treatise on Toleration, 1763
P16.translation: Translated by Joseph McCabe in Voltaire, Toleration and Other Essays (New York, 1912); the words in brackets are McCabe's; adapted

footnotes.text: battles of the French Wars of Religion, fought between Catholics and Huguenots (French Calvinists) from 1562 to 1587

glossary.d: the gentle patience of a father
wild, extreme belief that does not listen to reason
a member of the Greek Orthodox Church
members of small Protestant groups (the Memnonists are now called Mennonites)

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Bacon builds up from observed facts to general rules, while Descartes reasons step by step from clear ideas.
options.B: Bacon trusts the ancient philosophers as guides, while Descartes rejects the teachings of the ancient writers.
options.C: Bacon says mathematics is the key to knowledge, while Descartes says knowledge must come from experiments.
options.D: Bacon writes to defend religious faith, while Descartes writes to show that faith and reason cannot agree.

practice.explanation: Bacon wants people to climb "gradually" from facts gathered by the senses to general rules. This is called induction. Descartes wants to accept only what is clear beyond doubt and then reason in small steps, as in geometry. This is called deduction.

whyNot.B: Bacon does not praise the ancients. He calls the way "now in use" the wrong way and offers a new one.
whyNot.C: This mixes up the two writers. Descartes praises the "chains of simple and easy reasonings" used in geometry.
whyNot.D: Neither excerpt is about faith. Both are about how to find true knowledge.

practice.hint: Look at where each writer begins. Does Bacon start with facts or with big ideas? What does Descartes start with?

practice.stem: Both authors would most likely agree that

options.A: knowledge of nature should be studied mainly in the universities that trained the clergy and lawyers of Europe
options.B: mathematics is of little use to people who want to understand how nature works
options.C: scholars should follow a careful new method instead of accepting what earlier authorities taught
options.D: the senses are the most reliable guide to knowledge and do not need to be checked by reason

practice.explanation: Bacon and Descartes each offered a new way to find truth. Both refused to simply trust Aristotle and other old writers. That break with the past helped start the Scientific Revolution.

whyNot.A: Neither writer praises the universities of his day. Bacon says the usual way of finding truth is the wrong one.
whyNot.B: Descartes builds his method on the reasoning of geometers, so he would not agree.
whyNot.D: Descartes says to accept only what is clear beyond doubt, and Bacon's bee "works and fashions" what it gathers. Both want reason to check the senses.

practice.hint: Both men describe a way of thinking. What were they both trying to replace?

practice.stem: The methods described in the two sources contributed most directly to

options.A: the development of the scientific method, which joined careful observation and experiment with mathematics
options.B: a revival of Aristotle's ideas about nature in the universities of Europe during the 1700s
options.C: the Catholic Church's decision to accept the idea that the Earth moves around the Sun in the 1630s
options.D: the end of interest in alchemy and astrology among educated Europeans by the late 1600s

practice.explanation: Later scientists, such as Newton, used experiments, as Bacon urged, and mathematics, as Descartes urged. Together these ideas shaped the scientific method.

whyNot.B: Thinkers who used these new methods turned away from Aristotle's ideas about nature.
whyNot.C: In 1633 the Church put Galileo on trial for teaching that the Earth moves. It did not accept the idea then.
whyNot.D: Many educated people, including Isaac Newton, kept studying alchemy after 1650. Interest in it faded slowly.

practice.hint: One writer stresses facts from the senses and the other stresses math. What happens when you put them together?

practice.stem: Which evidence does Harvey use to support his idea that the blood moves in a circle?

options.A: Galen's writings describe the heart as a pump that moves blood through the whole body.
options.B: The amount of blood the heart sends out is too great to be made from the food a person eats.
options.C: Patients who had been bled by doctors reported that their pulse grew stronger afterward.
options.D: Ancient texts teach that blood, like water and air, follows the circular motion of the heavens.

practice.explanation: Harvey thought about how much blood passes through the heart and how fast. Food could not make that much new blood. So he decided that the same blood must return to the heart again and again.

whyNot.A: Harvey writes against the "respect for antiquity." He does not use Galen to support his idea.
whyNot.C: Harvey does not mention patients or bleeding. He reasons about how much blood the heart moves.
whyNot.D: Harvey says his idea is "novel and unheard-of." He does not claim ancient texts support it.

practice.hint: Reread the long sentence in the second paragraph. What did Harvey think about "the quantity of blood"?

practice.stem: Harvey's conclusion most directly challenged which earlier idea?

options.A: Vesalius's drawings of human anatomy, which were based on his own dissections of bodies
options.B: Paracelsus's view that sickness should be treated with medicines made from minerals
options.C: Galen's teaching that the liver keeps making new blood from food, which the body then uses up
options.D: Copernicus's argument that the Earth and the other planets move in circles around the Sun

practice.explanation: Galen, an ancient Greek doctor, taught that the liver made new blood from food and the body used it up. For about 1,400 years, doctors accepted his idea. Harvey showed that the same blood circulates.

whyNot.A: Vesalius also learned from dissections, as Harvey did. Harvey built on his work rather than challenging it.
whyNot.B: Paracelsus's medicines are a different topic. Harvey is writing about how blood moves.
whyNot.D: Copernicus wrote about the heavens, not the body. Harvey's "circle" is the path of the blood.

practice.hint: Harvey says food could not supply all that blood. Whose idea about where blood comes from does that go against?

practice.stem: Harvey's fear that "mankind at large" will be his enemies is best explained by

options.A: a ban by the Catholic Church on cutting open human bodies for medical study
options.B: Parliament's power to decide which books English physicians could publish and sell in London
options.C: the respect that physicians and universities still gave to ancient medical writers
options.D: a law in England that made it illegal to experiment on living animals

practice.explanation: In Harvey's time, doctors still learned medicine mostly from Galen and other ancient writers. Harvey says "wont and custom" and "respect for antiquity" shape what people believe. So he expected doctors to reject a new idea.

whyNot.A: Anatomists cut open human bodies in public lessons in this period. Vesalius had done so in Padua in the 1530s and 1540s.
whyNot.B: Harvey published his book in Frankfurt, in Latin. Parliament did not control what physicians printed.
whyNot.D: No such law existed. In his book, Harvey describes his own experiments on living animals.

practice.hint: Reread the words Harvey uses for why people will resist him: "wont," "custom," and "antiquity."

practice.stem: Voltaire's main purpose in comparing the treatment of Descartes and Newton was most likely to

options.A: criticize France by praising the freedom that English thinkers enjoyed
options.B: prove that Descartes's ideas about the universe were better than Newton's
options.C: warn English readers not to trust scientific ideas that came from France
options.D: persuade scientists to stay out of arguments about religion

practice.explanation: Voltaire shows that England buried Newton like a king, while Descartes was falsely called an atheist. He says Newton was lucky to live "in a country of liberty." Readers in France would see the contrast with their own country.

whyNot.B: Voltaire calls Newton the "destroyer of the Cartesian system." He sides with Newton's ideas.
whyNot.C: Voltaire was French and was writing mainly for French readers. He praises England, not France.
whyNot.D: Voltaire does not tell scientists to avoid religion. He says Descartes was unfairly attacked by religious critics.

practice.hint: Voltaire was a French writer. How would his French readers feel when he praised England?

practice.stem: Writers such as Voltaire contributed most directly to the Enlightenment by

options.A: carrying out the careful experiments that first proved Newton's laws of motion were correct
options.B: founding the Royal Society in London to pay for Newton's research
options.C: persuading the Catholic Church to teach Newton's physics in its schools in the 1730s
options.D: spreading Newton's ideas to a wide reading public and using them to question tradition

practice.explanation: Voltaire explained Newton's science in lively, easy language. He used it to show that reason could replace old beliefs. Writing like his helped carry the Scientific Revolution into the Enlightenment.

whyNot.A: Voltaire was a writer, not an experimenter. Newton and other scientists tested his laws.
whyNot.B: The Royal Society was founded in 1660, before Voltaire was born.
whyNot.C: The Church did not adopt Newton's physics in the 1730s. Voltaire's Letters were banned and burned in Paris in 1734.

practice.hint: Voltaire did not do science himself. What did he do with Newton's ideas?

practice.stem: The "attraction" that Voltaire says Newton used to explain nature refers to

options.A: magnetism, which Kepler thought might steer the planets in their paths around the Sun
options.B: inertia, a body's tendency to keep moving in a straight line
options.C: universal gravitation, a force by which all bodies pull on one another
options.D: the crystal spheres that carried the planets in Aristotle's universe

practice.explanation: Newton said the same force, gravity, pulls the Moon toward the Earth and the sea toward the Moon. Voltaire mentions the tides as an example. One set of laws explained motion on Earth and in the heavens.

whyNot.A: Kepler did wonder if a magnetic force moved the planets, but Newton's attraction is gravity.
whyNot.B: Inertia is one of Newton's ideas, but it is not a pull between bodies. It does not explain the tides.
whyNot.D: Crystal spheres were part of the old picture of the heavens that Newton's work replaced.

practice.hint: Think of Newton's most famous law. What does it say about the Moon and the Earth?

practice.stem: Locke's main argument in the passage is that

options.A: kings receive their power directly from God and answer to God, not their subjects, for how they rule
options.B: governments get their power from the people's consent and lose it if they abuse that power
options.C: people living without a government follow no rules and have no rights that others must respect
options.D: a ruler with complete power is needed to keep people from falling into a constant war against one another

practice.explanation: Locke says people are born "free, equal, and independent." They join a government only by their own consent, to protect their lives, liberty, and property. If rulers attack those rights, the people may set up a new government.

whyNot.A: This is the divine-right idea of writers like Bishop Bossuet. Locke says power comes from "consent."
whyNot.C: Locke says the state of nature has "a law of nature to govern it."
whyNot.D: This is close to Thomas Hobbes's view. Locke says the people may resist rulers who use "arbitrary power."

practice.hint: Find the word Locke uses for how a person comes under someone's political power.

practice.stem: Locke's ideas in the passage were most directly shaped by

options.A: the Thirty Years' War between Catholic and Protestant states in the Holy Roman Empire
options.B: Louis XIV's efforts to bring the French nobles under his control at Versailles
options.C: conflicts in England over whether Parliament or the Stuart kings held supreme power
options.D: the revolt of the Dutch provinces against the rule of the Spanish king in the 1500s

practice.explanation: England fought a civil war in the 1640s over the king's power. In the Glorious Revolution of 1688, Parliament replaced James II with William and Mary. Locke's book, published in 1690, was used to defend that change.

whyNot.A: The Thirty Years' War ended in 1648. Locke's arguments respond to quarrels between English kings and Parliament.
whyNot.B: Louis XIV built strong royal power in France. Locke is answering a question that divided England.
whyNot.D: The Dutch Revolt began a century before Locke wrote. English events in the 1600s mattered far more to him.

practice.hint: Locke was English, and his book came out in 1690. What had just happened to England's king?

practice.stem: Ideas like those in the passage were later used most directly to justify

options.A: the American and French revolutions in the late 1700s
options.B: Frederick II's claim that a king is the first servant of the state
options.C: Louis XIV's decision to end the toleration of French Protestants
options.D: Catherine II's plan for a new law code to strengthen her rule

practice.explanation: Locke's ideas about natural rights and consent show up in the Declaration of Independence of 1776. They also show up in France's Declaration of the Rights of Man of 1789. Both revolutions claimed the people could replace a government that broke their trust.

whyNot.B: Frederick kept full power for himself. He did not say the people could replace their ruler.
whyNot.C: Louis XIV took rights away from Protestants in 1685. That is the kind of rule Locke opposed.
whyNot.D: Catherine kept absolute power for herself. Locke argued that rulers who abuse their power can be replaced.

practice.hint: Locke says the people may set up "a new legislative." When did people in the late 1700s do that?

practice.stem: According to Montesquieu, liberty depends on

options.A: giving the powers of government to a single assembly elected by the people
options.B: letting judges make the laws so that kings cannot act like tyrants
options.C: keeping the powers to make, carry out, and judge laws in separate hands
options.D: placing power in the hands of a wise prince who governs by reason and justice

practice.explanation: Montesquieu describes three powers: making laws, carrying them out, and judging cases. He says that when one person or group holds them all, tyranny follows. This idea is called the separation of powers.

whyNot.A: Montesquieu warns against giving the three powers to one body, "whether of the nobles or of the people."
whyNot.B: He says liberty is lost if the judge becomes the lawmaker.
whyNot.D: He says there is "no liberty" when one person holds both the lawmaking and the executive powers.

practice.hint: What does Montesquieu say happens when the powers are "united"?

practice.stem: Montesquieu's description of "Turkey" most directly reflects

options.A: a European tendency to picture Asian empires as examples of tyranny
options.B: what Montesquieu learned while serving as France's ambassador in Istanbul
options.C: the Ottoman sultan's recent decision to share power with an elected parliament
options.D: the Ottoman Empire's defeat of the Habsburg army outside Vienna in 1683

practice.explanation: European writers often used Asian empires as a picture of what they feared at home. Montesquieu calls the Ottoman sultan a ruler whose subjects "groan" under oppression. He knew the empire only from books and travelers' reports.

whyNot.B: Montesquieu never served as an ambassador and never went to the Ottoman Empire. He knew it only from books and travelers' reports.
whyNot.C: The Ottoman Empire did not have an elected parliament until 1876.
whyNot.D: The Ottomans lost the battle at Vienna in 1683. Their defeat does not explain Montesquieu's description.

practice.hint: Think about how European writers of the 1700s often described rulers in Asia.

practice.stem: Montesquieu's ideas in the passage most directly influenced

options.A: Catherine II's decision to share her power with an elected Russian assembly
options.B: the Physiocrats' call to free the grain trade from government rules in France
options.C: the English Parliament's decision after 1689 to let the king make laws without its approval
options.D: the writers of the United States Constitution, who divided power among three branches

practice.explanation: The United States Constitution of 1787 split power among Congress, the president, and the courts. Its writers often quoted Montesquieu. They hoped that dividing power would protect liberty.

whyNot.A: Catherine's 1767 commission only gave her advice on laws. She kept her absolute power.
whyNot.B: The Physiocrats wrote about trade and farming. Montesquieu writes about how to divide the power of government.
whyNot.C: Parliament did not give up its lawmaking power. After 1689, kings needed Parliament's approval for laws.

practice.hint: Think about which later lawmakers said they had read The Spirit of the Laws.

practice.stem: Beccaria's argument best reflects the Enlightenment belief that

options.A: punishments should match how sinful a crime is in the eyes of God and the Church
options.B: the best laws are the oldest ones, because custom shows what has worked over time
options.C: people accused of crimes should be tried by courts made up of nobles and clergy
options.D: laws and punishments should be judged by reason and by how well they serve society

practice.explanation: Beccaria asks what punishment is for. He says its purpose is to prevent crime, not to cause pain. He uses reason to show that torture and the death penalty do more harm than good.

whyNot.A: Beccaria does not judge crimes as sins. He asks what punishment is useful for society.
whyNot.B: Beccaria says that custom has kept cruel practices like torture alive. He wants to test laws by reason.
whyNot.C: Beccaria says nothing about who should sit on the courts. He writes about the purpose of punishment.

practice.hint: Beccaria asks whether punishments are useful. What does that tell you about how he tests a law?

practice.stem: Beccaria's praise of the "benevolent monarchs" on Europe's thrones suggests that he hoped

options.A: the people would overthrow kings who refused to change the laws
options.B: the Catholic Church would take control of the criminal courts
options.C: powerful rulers would use their power to make his reforms
options.D: elected assemblies would soon replace kings as the lawmakers of Europe's states

practice.explanation: Many Enlightenment writers hoped that strong rulers would make reforms from the top. Beccaria calls Europe's kings "fathers of their people." He wanted them to rewrite the laws.

whyNot.A: Beccaria praises Europe's monarchs. He does not call for revolution.
whyNot.B: Beccaria wants laws based on reason, not control by the Church.
whyNot.D: Beccaria praises the monarchs themselves. He does not ask for assemblies to take their place.

practice.hint: Beccaria calls the monarchs "benevolent." What did he want them to do with their power?

practice.stem: Which of the following most directly reflects the influence of ideas like Beccaria's?

options.A: Frederick II's order bringing back torture in Prussian courts during the Seven Years' War
options.B: Louis XV's use of royal orders to jail critics in France without any trial
options.C: England's increase in the number of crimes punished by death in the 1700s
options.D: Joseph II's law code of 1787, which ended the death penalty for most crimes in Austria

practice.explanation: Beccaria's book was read across Europe. Enlightened rulers changed their laws. Leopold of Tuscany ended the death penalty in 1786, and his brother Joseph II limited it in Austria in 1787.

whyNot.A: Frederick II abolished torture in most cases soon after he became king in 1740. He did not bring it back.
whyNot.B: Jailing people without trial goes against Beccaria's rule that no one is a criminal until found guilty.
whyNot.C: England's harsh laws went in the opposite direction from Beccaria's ideas.

practice.hint: Beccaria opposed torture and the death penalty. Did each ruler follow or reject that advice?

practice.stem: The gatherings Marmontel describes are best understood as an example of

options.A: academies of science, which monarchs set up to pay for research
options.B: Masonic lodges, where members swore to keep their meetings secret
options.C: salons, where hosts brought writers, artists, and nobles together to talk
options.D: lending libraries, which let readers borrow books for a small fee

practice.explanation: In Paris, wealthy women hosted salons in their homes. Writers, artists, and nobles met there to share and debate ideas. Madame Geoffrin's salon was one of the most famous.

whyNot.A: Royal academies were official bodies. Madame Geoffrin's dinners took place in her own home.
whyNot.B: Masonic lodges were clubs with secret rituals. Marmontel describes open dinners hosted by a woman.
whyNot.D: A library lends books. Marmontel describes dinners where guests talked.

practice.hint: Who is the host, and where do the guests meet?

practice.stem: Marmontel suggests that Madame Geoffrin's main skill as a host was

options.A: keeping the talk lively while making sure it stayed within limits
options.B: explaining the newest scientific theories to her guests over dinner each week
options.C: protecting her guests from arrest by the king's censors
options.D: writing reviews of her guests' books for Paris journals

practice.explanation: Marmontel says her "great art" was "presiding" over guests who loved freedom. With a word or a gesture she pulled back anyone who went too far. She let people talk but kept order.

whyNot.B: Marmontel says she had "no knowledge either of the arts or of literature."
whyNot.C: The passage does not mention censors or arrests.
whyNot.D: Marmontel does not say she wrote anything. He praises how she ran the conversation.

practice.hint: Find the words "her great art." What does Marmontel say comes next?

practice.stem: Gatherings like the ones Marmontel describes contributed to the Enlightenment mainly by

options.A: giving some wealthy women a leading role in sharing new ideas
options.B: replacing printed books and journals as the main way new ideas reached readers
options.C: keeping talk about new ideas inside the king's court at Versailles
options.D: ending the French government's censorship of books and newspapers

practice.explanation: Salon hostesses chose the guests and guided the talk. Through their salons, women such as Madame Geoffrin helped spread new ideas, even though they were shut out of universities and politics.

whyNot.B: Salon guests discussed books and journals. Salons added to print; they did not replace it.
whyNot.C: Salons met in private homes in Paris. Marmontel says Madame Geoffrin drew the great to her own house.
whyNot.D: France still censored books. The Encyclopédie was banned in 1759.

practice.hint: Who ran these gatherings, and what part did she play?

practice.stem: Macaulay's main claim about the coffee houses is that they

options.A: were set up by the king's government to spread official news among the people of London and Westminster
options.B: were meant for nobles and great merchants who could pay high prices for coffee
options.C: were places where public opinion was formed and voiced at a time when other outlets were missing
options.D: served mainly as offices where merchants arranged trade with the Ottoman Empire

practice.explanation: Macaulay says that in 1685 there was no Parliament meeting and no real newspaper. So Londoners met in coffee houses to share news and argue about politics. He calls them "the chief organs" of public opinion.

whyNot.A: Macaulay says the Court was uneasy about the coffee houses and once tried to close them.
whyNot.B: Macaulay says anyone who paid "his penny at the bar" could come in.
whyNot.D: The first coffee house was started by a Turkey merchant, but Macaulay says people came to discuss the news.

practice.hint: Look at the end of the first paragraph. What does Macaulay call the coffee houses?

practice.stem: The rise of the coffee houses Macaulay describes was made possible in part by

options.A: the Agricultural Revolution, which had freed most English workers from farm labor by the 1680s
options.B: the growth of European trade with Asia, Africa, and the Americas, which brought new goods
options.C: the repeal of the Navigation Acts, which had limited the goods that could enter England
options.D: Charles II's laws encouraging his subjects to debate politics in public places

practice.explanation: Coffee came to Europe through trade with the Ottoman Empire, and later from colonies in Asia and the Americas. Growing trade made coffee, tea, sugar, and tobacco cheap enough for many people. That helped coffee houses spread.

whyNot.A: In the 1680s most English people still worked on farms. The big changes in farming came later.
whyNot.C: The Navigation Acts stayed in force until 1849.
whyNot.D: Macaulay says the Court tried to close the coffee houses, not encourage them.

practice.hint: Where did the coffee come from? How did it get to London?

practice.stem: In the 1700s, places like the coffee houses Macaulay describes contributed most directly to

options.A: a decline in London's importance as a center of trade and banking
options.B: the end of censorship in most countries of continental Europe
options.C: the growth of Puritan opposition to the Church of England
options.D: the spread of Enlightenment ideas through print and conversation

practice.explanation: Coffee houses kept newspapers and journals for customers to read. People there discussed new books and ideas. This helped carry the Enlightenment beyond a small group of thinkers.

whyNot.A: London grew as a center of trade and banking in the 1700s. Merchants often did business in coffee houses.
whyNot.B: Censorship lasted in France, Austria, and other countries through the 1700s.
whyNot.C: Macaulay says every religious group had its own coffee houses, but the Puritans' main fight with the Church of England came earlier, in the 1600s.

practice.hint: What did people do in the coffee houses besides drink coffee?

practice.stem: Hume's main argument is that

options.A: a love of comfort and fine goods makes people more hard-working, sociable, and knowledgeable
options.B: luxury makes people lazy and selfish and in time weakens the nation that allows it
options.C: governments should limit the import of foreign luxury goods to protect their own workers
options.D: learning grows best in simple farming societies where people live apart from one another

practice.explanation: Hume says industry, knowledge, and humanity are "linked together." When people make and buy fine goods, they also meet in clubs, share ideas, and treat one another better. He defends luxury against those who called it sinful.

whyNot.B: Hume argues the opposite. He says the "luxurious ages" are the ones with the most industry and humanity.
whyNot.C: Hume does not discuss trade rules or imports.
whyNot.D: Hume says people grow more sociable and learned when they "flock into cities."

practice.hint: Hume names three things that are "linked together." What are they?

practice.stem: Hume's essay is best understood in the context of

options.A: new guild rules in British towns that limited how many goods craftsmen could make and sell
options.B: a consumer revolution in which more families bought goods such as mirrors and porcelain
options.C: laws in Britain that limited silk and other costly fabrics to the nobility
options.D: a long drop in British trade caused by the wars of Louis XIV against the Dutch

practice.explanation: In the 1700s, more middle-class families could buy new goods for their homes, such as porcelain dishes, cotton cloth, and mirrors. Hume mentions people showing their taste "in clothes or furniture." His essay defends this new way of living.

whyNot.A: Guilds were losing power in Britain in the 1700s. Trade and crafts were growing more free.
whyNot.C: Laws like this, called sumptuary laws, had mostly faded in Britain by the 1700s, as more people bought fine goods.
whyNot.D: British trade grew after 1713. Hume writes about a time of growing wealth.

practice.hint: Hume mentions "clothes or furniture." What was happening to what people bought in the 1700s?

practice.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most challenge Hume's claim that refinement leads people to "indulge" less in excess?

options.A: Reading clubs and debating societies spread to many British towns during the 1700s.
options.B: Britain fought several wars against France for colonies and trade during the 1700s.
options.C: Potters such as Josiah Wedgwood made fine plates and vases for middle-class buyers.
options.D: Gin drinking and crime rose sharply among London's poor in the 1730s and 1740s.

practice.explanation: Hume says that the more people refine their pleasures, "the less will they indulge in excesses of any kind." But in London in the 1730s and 1740s, cheap gin caused drunkenness, crime, and many deaths. That evidence goes against his claim.

whyNot.A: Reading clubs fit Hume's claim that "clubs and societies are everywhere formed."
whyNot.B: These wars are true, but they do not show whether city people grew more or less excessive in their habits.
whyNot.C: Fine pottery for middle-class buyers fits Hume's picture of refined taste spreading.

practice.hint: First decide what Hume predicts about how people behave in cities. Then test each choice against that prediction.

practice.stem: The painting is an example of which artistic style?

options.A: Baroque art, which used drama, motion, and rich color to glorify the Church and kings
options.B: Neoclassicism, which used stories from ancient Greece and Rome to teach civic virtue
options.C: Romanticism, which celebrated strong feeling, wild nature, and the individual
options.D: Rococo art, which showed playful scenes of nobles enjoying love and leisure

practice.explanation: Neoclassical artists copied the clean lines and plain settings of ancient art. David chose a story from early Rome. The brothers' oath shows citizens putting their country first.

whyNot.A: Baroque artists, such as Bernini and Rubens, filled scenes with swirling motion and showed saints or kings. David's scene is calm, plain, and taken from Roman history.
whyNot.C: Romantic painters came later, in the early 1800s, and often showed wild nature. David shows a planned, orderly scene of duty.
whyNot.D: Rococo paintings show light, playful scenes of aristocrats. David's painting is serious and stern.

practice.hint: Look at the clothing, the setting, and the story in the title. What time period do they come from?

practice.stem: In the 1780s, paintings like this one most directly expressed which idea?

options.A: celebrating the private comforts of family life inside the home
options.B: loyalty to the king as the father of the nation and its protector
options.C: admiration for the simple, natural life of peasants far from cities
options.D: praising citizens who put duty to their country ahead of their own lives

practice.explanation: Enlightenment writers talked about citizenship and the public good. Neoclassical artists showed heroes from Greece and Rome who served their country. David's brothers swear to fight to the death for Rome.

whyNot.A: The weeping women show family life, but the painting praises the men who leave it for their country.
whyNot.B: No king appears in the painting. The brothers swear loyalty to Rome itself, not to a ruler.
whyNot.C: The painting shows Roman warriors taking an oath in a stone hall, not peasants in the countryside.

practice.hint: What are the brothers promising? Who are they promising it for?

practice.stem: Compared with much European art of the 1600s, the painting shows a shift toward

options.A: scenes of the everyday lives of peasants and workers rather than stories about ancient heroes
options.B: the use of religious symbols to support the Catholic Church against Protestants
options.C: large paintings made for church altars rather than for public exhibitions
options.D: calm, orderly scenes of public virtue instead of religious glory and royal splendor

practice.explanation: Much art of the 1600s was Baroque: dramatic, crowded, and made to glorify the Church or kings. By the 1780s, Neoclassical painters used calm, simple scenes. Their subject was the duty of citizens.

whyNot.A: David's painting shows ancient Roman heroes, not peasants.
whyNot.B: The painting has no religious symbols. Supporting the Church was a goal of Baroque art in the 1600s.
whyNot.C: The painting was shown in a public exhibition in Paris, not placed on a church altar.

practice.hint: Think about what Baroque art showed. What is different about David's subject and style?

practice.stem: The practice Montagu describes is most directly connected to which 18th-century development?

options.A: the disappearance of the plague as a major epidemic disease in western Europe
options.B: the germ theory, which showed that tiny living things cause disease
options.C: the spread of inoculation, which lowered the number of deaths from smallpox
options.D: Harvey's discovery that the heart pumps blood around the body

practice.explanation: The old women put a little matter from a mild smallpox sore into a cut. The person caught a mild case and was then safe from the deadly kind. This is called inoculation. Montagu helped bring it to England in the 1720s.

whyNot.A: Plague did fade in the 1700s, but Montagu is writing about smallpox.
whyNot.B: Germ theory came in the late 1800s, long after this letter.
whyNot.D: Harvey's work on the blood came about 90 years earlier and is not about smallpox.

practice.hint: What does the old woman put into the cut? What happens to the patients afterward?

practice.stem: Montagu's comment about English doctors suggests that she expected them to

options.A: reject the practice because it came from the Muslim Ottoman Empire
options.B: resist the practice because it would cut their income
options.C: ask the Church of England to ban the practice as sinful
options.D: urge Parliament to make the practice a legal requirement

practice.explanation: Montagu says smallpox is "a considerable branch" of doctors' "revenue." Treating smallpox earned doctors money. She doubted they would support a practice that might put an end to the disease.

whyNot.A: Some critics did call inoculation a foreign custom. But Montagu says the doctors would lose money.
whyNot.C: Montagu does not mention the Church. She talks about the doctors' "revenue."
whyNot.D: Montagu expects the doctors to oppose the practice, not to demand it.

practice.hint: Reread the last sentence. What does Montagu say doctors would lose?

practice.stem: Montagu's letter is an example of how, in the 1700s,

options.A: European rulers sent doctors to study medicine at universities in Asia and Africa
options.B: travel writing exposed Europeans to the practices and customs of peoples outside Europe
options.C: European scientists rejected any practice that did not appear in ancient Greek texts
options.D: Ottoman sultans spread new medical practices to Europe through official treaties

practice.explanation: Letters and travel books by Europeans abroad were popular in the 1700s. They showed readers how people in other places lived. Some of these writings, like Montagu's, challenged European ideas.

whyNot.A: Montagu learned about the practice while she lived in the Ottoman Empire. No doctors were sent there to study it.
whyNot.C: Many Europeans were curious about practices from other places. Inoculation spread in Britain in the 1720s.
whyNot.D: Montagu learned of the practice from local people, not from the sultan or any treaty.

practice.hint: Where was Montagu living, and who was she writing to?

practice.stem: Prothero's main argument about English farming in the 1700s is that it

options.A: produced far more food, but at a heavy cost to small farmers
options.B: changed very little until farm machines came into use in the middle of the 1800s
options.C: improved mainly because peasants gained secure ownership of the land they farmed
options.D: fell into crisis as the new methods caused repeated famines across England

practice.explanation: Prothero praises the new crops, methods, and animal breeding that fed a growing population. But he says the changes pushed small farmers and villagers off the land. That was "the heavy price" of more food.

whyNot.B: Prothero calls the change between 1700 and 1800 "astonishing."
whyNot.C: Prothero says the opposite: the peasantry was divorced "from the soil."
whyNot.D: Prothero says England produced more food and became "the granary of Europe."

practice.hint: Prothero praises the changes but also names a "heavy price." Find both parts.

practice.stem: The change from "common cultivation" to "separate occupation" that Prothero describes refers to

options.A: enclosure, in which open fields and common lands were fenced into private farms
options.B: the end of serfdom, which freed English peasants from forced labor for their lords
options.C: the putting-out system, in which merchants paid rural families to make cloth at home
options.D: crop rotation, in which farmers planted turnips and clover instead of leaving fields empty

practice.explanation: Under the old system, villagers farmed strips in big open fields and shared the commons. Enclosure replaced these with fenced farms held by one owner or tenant. Landowners often got Parliament to pass enclosure acts.

whyNot.B: Serfdom had faded in England centuries earlier, by about 1500.
whyNot.C: The putting-out system was about making cloth, not about who farmed the land.
whyNot.D: Crop rotation was one of the new methods, but it is not a change in who held and worked the land.

practice.hint: Compare the two glossary entries. What changed about who controlled the land?

practice.stem: The "divorce of the peasantry from the soil" that Prothero describes contributed most directly to

options.A: a fall in England's population during the second half of the 1700s
options.B: the creation of England's first poor laws to help people who had no work
options.C: the spread of serfdom to farm workers in Britain and other parts of western Europe
options.D: the movement of rural people into towns and cities in search of work

practice.explanation: When villagers lost their land and common rights, many had to work for wages. Farms now needed fewer workers. So many people moved to towns and cities, where new industries needed workers.

whyNot.A: England's population grew quickly in the late 1700s.
whyNot.B: England's main poor law was passed in 1601, and earlier ones date from the 1500s, long before these changes.
whyNot.C: Serfdom spread in eastern Europe, not western Europe, and it had grown there earlier.

practice.hint: If people lost their land, how would they earn a living? Where could they go?

practice.stem: Hogarth most likely made this print in order to

options.A: advertise the gin sold by London's distillers and gin shops
options.B: support efforts to limit the sale of cheap gin to London's poor
options.C: argue that the poor should be moved out of London to farms
options.D: criticize the Church of England for ignoring the city's poor

practice.explanation: Hogarth shows gin causing neglect, poverty, and death. He made the print in 1751, the year Parliament passed a law to raise taxes on gin and limit who could sell it. He wanted his print to push people to support that law.

whyNot.A: Every scene shows harm from gin, so the print is not an advertisement.
whyNot.C: The print shows the harm of drinking. It does not suggest moving people to farms.
whyNot.D: A church steeple appears in the distance, but the print blames gin for the ruin in the street.

practice.hint: Is anything in the picture going well? What does Hogarth blame?

practice.stem: The scene in the print is best understood in the context of

options.A: the return of the plague to London in a great outbreak in the 1740s
options.B: the collapse of English farming in the decades after the Seven Years' War
options.C: the rapid growth of cities, which drew poor migrants from the countryside
options.D: the destruction of much of London by the Great Fire of 1666 and the slow rebuilding

practice.explanation: In the 1700s, many poor people moved from the countryside to London to find work. The city grew crowded, and many lived in poverty. Cheap gin spread quickly in these crowded neighborhoods.

whyNot.A: London's last great plague was in 1665. Plague faded from western Europe in the 1700s.
whyNot.B: The Seven Years' War began in 1756, after this print, and English farming grew in this period.
whyNot.D: The Great Fire came almost a century earlier. The ruined houses in the print show poverty and neglect.

practice.hint: Who lived in the crowded streets of London? Where had many of them come from?

practice.stem: Worries like those shown in the print most directly led to

options.A: greater efforts by governments and reformers to police and control the urban poor
options.B: the British government taking over the gin distilleries of London and running them itself
options.C: a British law of the 1750s that set up free public schools in London
options.D: a sharp drop in the number of people moving from the countryside to London

practice.explanation: Crowded cities made poverty, crime, and drinking easy to see. In response, Parliament passed laws on gin, and London set up stronger watchmen and magistrates. Reformers also opened workhouses and charities to control the poor.

whyNot.B: Parliament taxed and licensed gin sellers. It did not take over the distilleries.
whyNot.C: Britain did not set up free public schools for all children until the late 1800s.
whyNot.D: People kept moving to London and other cities for work. London kept growing.

practice.hint: The print shows crime and disorder. What would leaders want to do about it?

practice.stem: Frederick's description of a ruler's duties best reflects

options.A: constitutional monarchy, in which an elected parliament limits the power of the king
options.B: divine-right monarchy, in which the king is responsible to God and not to his subjects
options.C: enlightened absolutism, in which a ruler with full power claimed to serve the state
options.D: republicanism, in which citizens choose their leaders and can vote them out

practice.explanation: Frederick kept full control of Prussia. But he said a king must serve the state: keep the laws, help farming and trade, and spend taxes wisely. Rulers who mixed full power with Enlightenment ideas are called enlightened absolutists.

whyNot.A: Frederick does not mention a parliament or any limits on his power.
whyNot.B: Frederick bases royal power on men who chose "one of their equals," not on God.
whyNot.D: Frederick defends monarchy. He does not want citizens to elect their leaders.

practice.hint: Does Frederick share power with anyone? What does he say the ruler is for?

practice.stem: Frederick's idea that rulers were first chosen by "their equals" differs from older defenses of royal power in that it

options.A: says that the nobles should elect each new king when the old king dies
options.B: explains royal power as a duty owed to the people rather than a gift from God
options.C: denies that a king has any right to collect taxes from his subjects
options.D: argues that the Church must approve each new king before he can rule

practice.explanation: Older writers, such as Bishop Bossuet, said kings got their power from God. Frederick says people gave power to one ruler so he would serve them. He calls the king "the first servant of the State."

whyNot.A: Frederick says nothing about electing kings. He was a hereditary king.
whyNot.C: Frederick says the army and government need money. He wants taxes used wisely, not ended.
whyNot.D: Frederick does not mention the Church. His argument is based on service to the state.

practice.hint: Where does Frederick say a ruler's power came from? Where did Bossuet say it came from?

practice.stem: Frederick's focus on the army, finances, and the "enemies of the State" is best understood in the context of

options.A: Prussia's growth into a great power in a Holy Roman Empire weakened after 1648
options.B: Prussia's loss of its eastern lands to Russia at the end of the Great Northern War in 1721
options.C: the Habsburgs' loss of Hungary to the Ottoman Empire after the siege of Vienna in 1683
options.D: the Diplomatic Revolution of 1756, in which Prussia joined France against Britain

practice.explanation: After 1648, the princes of the Holy Roman Empire ran their own states. Prussia's kings built a large army and a careful tax system. Frederick seized Silesia from Austria in 1740 and kept it, which made Prussia a great power.

whyNot.B: Prussia did not lose its eastern lands to Russia. It gained land in the 1700s.
whyNot.C: The Habsburgs defeated the Ottomans at Vienna in 1683 and took Hungary from them by 1699.
whyNot.D: In 1756 Prussia allied with Britain, while Austria allied with its old enemy, France.

practice.hint: Prussia was small but had a very large army. Who did Frederick fight, and why did he need money?

practice.stem: Necker's main claim is that public opinion in France

options.A: was controlled by the king through his guards, his armies, and the royal treasury
options.B: acted as a check on the abuse of power even though it had no legal authority
options.C: had less power in France than in other countries of Europe
options.D: should be replaced by an elected assembly that would make France's laws

practice.explanation: Necker calls public opinion "an invisible power." It had no army or money, yet even the king's court paid attention to it. Necker says it did more than anything else to stop the abuse of power.

whyNot.A: Necker says public opinion is "destitute of treasury, of guards and armies." The king did not control it.
whyNot.C: Necker says foreigners cannot understand how strong public opinion is in France.
whyNot.D: Necker does not call for an elected assembly. He praises public opinion as it is.

practice.hint: Necker calls public opinion a kind of power. What does it do, and what does it lack?

practice.stem: Necker's view of public opinion was most likely shaped by his experience as

options.A: a minister who had won the Parlement's approval for new taxes on nobles
options.B: a banker who had grown rich collecting the king's taxes as a tax farmer
options.C: a minister who had governed France while the young king was a child
options.D: a royal minister who had published a report on the king's finances

practice.explanation: In 1781, Necker published a report on the king's finances for the public to read. It sold many copies. He knew that his power as a minister depended on the public's trust.

whyNot.A: Necker avoided new taxes and paid for France's costs with loans. Later ministers who tried to tax the nobles were blocked.
whyNot.B: Necker made his fortune as a private banker. Tax farmers were a separate group of financiers whom many people hated.
whyNot.C: Louis XVI was 19 when he became king in 1774. A regent ruled for Louis XV, not Louis XVI.

practice.hint: Read the attribution. What job did Necker have, and what would he need from the public?

practice.stem: The power of public opinion that Necker describes grew most directly out of

options.A: the regular meetings of the Estates General throughout the 1700s
options.B: Louis XV's creation of an elected national assembly in the 1760s
options.C: the French government's decision to end the censorship of books in the 1750s
options.D: the spread of newspapers and pamphlets and of places to discuss them

practice.explanation: In the 1700s, more French people could read. Newspapers, pamphlets, and books spread. People talked about them in cafés and salons. This created a public that judged the king's government.

whyNot.A: The Estates General did not meet from 1614 to 1789.
whyNot.B: No French king created an elected assembly before 1789.
whyNot.C: France kept censoring books until the Revolution. The Encyclopédie was banned in 1759.

practice.hint: Necker says public opinion had no army or treasury. Where did its power come from?

practice.stem: Voltaire's main argument in the passage is that

options.A: Protestants should be forced to become Catholics so that France would have one religion
options.B: France could now safely tolerate its Protestants
options.C: tolerating Protestants would bring back civil wars like those of the 1500s
options.D: churches should be closed and replaced by the study of science
